{
  "segment_function": "The block explains how speech and action reveal the unique identity of the agent within human togetherness and why action loses this revelatory quality when reduced to a means-end activity.",
  "claims": [
    {
      "claim": "The revelatory quality of speech and action emerges in sheer human togetherness where people are neither for nor against each other.",
      "claim_type": "author_position",
      "supporting_excerpt": "This revelatory quality of speech and action comes to the fore where people are with others and neither for nor against them—that is, in sheer human togetherness.",
      "support_kind": "direct",
      "confidence": 1.0
    },
    {
      "claim": "Attempting to verbalize who someone is inevitably leads to describing what they are in terms of shared qualities, causing their specific uniqueness to escape.",
      "claim_type": "author_position",
      "supporting_excerpt": "The moment we want to say who somebody is, our very vocabulary leads us astray into saying what he is; we get entangled in a description of qualities he necessarily shares with others like him; we begin to describe a type or a “character” in the old meaning of the word, with the result that his specific uniqueness escapes us.",
      "support_kind": "direct",
      "confidence": 1.0
    }
  ],
  "definitions": [],
  "distinctions": [],
  "references_to_other_sections": [],
  "unresolved_context": [],
  "must_not_be_lost": [
    "Action requires the public realm and the disclosure of the agent ('who') rather than merely the achievement ('what').",
    "Human affairs inherently lack the stability and tangibility of things because they are driven by the unreliable manifestations of acting and speaking beings."
  ]
}
